reading.body:
Lenovo's US arm filed 10 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports naming AI, spread across 16 different bills and seven named lobbyists.

The pattern is breadth, not depth. Sixteen bills is a wide net for a single client, and the filings name both House and Senate measures. The lobbyist list is concentrated at the top, with Jon Beamer on all 10 filings and Heather Smith on 9, then a long tail of five others on five or fewer. That shape suggests a small core team carrying the account, with additional names rotated in for specific issues.

For AI specifically, this is the input side of the policy pipeline. Compute scaling depends on buildings, power, and the rules that govern where they get built and how they operate. A hardware manufacturer lobbying on 16 AI-related bills is a signal that the legislative surface touching AI hardware is already wide, and that firms in this position treat it as a standing portfolio rather than a single-issue campaign.

What the data does not say is what Lenovo argued. A filing reports that a firm lobbied on an issue, not the position taken, so nothing here indicates whether the company supported or opposed any of these bills. The filings also do not show spending amounts, outcomes, or whether the named lobbyists actually met with anyone. The bill numbers are listed without titles, so the subject matter of each measure is not visible in this data.
